JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he would not watch it

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Figure caption,

"I'm not going to be watching it" - JD Vance on possible livestreamed execution

By Nardine Saad and Kali Hays

Published

9 October 2026

JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution.

The US vice-president expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the December execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added that "if it's through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it".

Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.

Nidal Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009 and injured another 32. His execution would be the first military firing squad execution in more than 60 years.

The Pentagon announced its desire to execute the former US Army major by firing squad over the attack on 3 December earlier this week.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth then said the execution would be livestreamed for the public, as "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".

Trump was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists as he left the White House on Friday.

Calling Hasan "totally nuts", he replied: "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

The Pentagon declined to comment further when asked for more information about a decision on the livestream.

Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" while speaking to reporters on Friday.

Asked about how his Catholic faith affected his stance on the plan to stream a public execution, Vance questioned whether it would happen.

But he noted that Hasan, a military psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems, but had instead "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived".

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Figure caption,

Watch: Trump says he approved the livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter

The possible livestreaming of the execution has been met with criticism from both political parties.

Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched, warning that public executions eroded civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment".

Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider.

"The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent."

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.

Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that while he "absolutely" supported the death sentence, livestreaming executions was "what jihadists do - America is better than that".

John Bolton, a former national security adviser during the first Trump administration, told BBC's Radio 4 PM that he supported capital punishment, but that the livestream was "unnecessary" because there were provisions for interested parties to view the execution in person.

"I just think this is a mark by Secretary Hegseth doing something he thinks will please President Trump," he said. "I think that's really not appropriate for a secretary of defence."

The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow".

The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Figure caption,

Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?

Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines on 5 November 2009.

He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.

It was the deadliest ever non-combat attack on a US military base.

While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.

When Hegseth told reporters on Thursday about his livestreaming plans, he did not specify where or how the execution would be shown.

A Pentagon spokesperson later reiterated to the BBC that Hasan's execution "will be livestreamed" but said the government had no further details.

The White House did not respond to an inquiry about whether it expected to show Hasan's planned execution on its social media channels.

Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says

Published

1 day ago

Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream

Published

2 days ago

All of the social media platforms the US government has accounts on have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence.

Meta - owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads - explicitly bans any livestream of capital punishment.

YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers", while TikTok similarly bars "extremely graphic, violent or disturbing content" that includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual".

But both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest".

Asked whether a livestream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned, a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach."

The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" violence.

Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment.

Embraer, Lockheed Martin vie for India’s $10.5B military transport aircraft deal

By Anjana Pasricha

Wednesday, Oct 7, 2026

An Indian Air Force C-130J Super Hercules aircraft is on display at the Hindon Airbase in Ghaziabad, India, on Oct. 8, 2025. (Sakib Ali/Hindustan Times via Getty Images)

NEW DELHI — Global aerospace companies Embraer from Brazil and Lockheed Martin from the United States are offering to expand aircraft manufacturing facilities in India as they pursue an approximately $10.5 billion contract for 60 medium transport aircraft for the Indian Air Force.

Embraer’s C-390 Millennium is competing with Lockheed Martin’s C-130J Super Hercules as India seeks to replace its aging military transport fleet that includes the Soviet-era Antonov An-32.

The formal race for one of India’s biggest military aviation contracts set off in August when India issued a Request for Proposal to five Indian companies setting the stage for the bidding. Global aviation companies are partnering with Indian firms because New Delhi has mandated that while the initial multi role aircraft will be delivered ready to fly, the rest must be built domestically .

With India’s focus on building a local aerospace industrial base, Embraer announced on Oct. 1 that the company and its Indian partner, Mahindra Defence, have identified the central Indian city of Nagpur as a production site for the aircraft if they are awarded the contract.

“Identifying Nagpur as a potential location for an assembly facility is an important step in building a robust, long-term aerospace ecosystem in the country,” said Bosco da Costa Junior, president and CEO of Embraer Defense & Security, in a joint statement with Mahindra.

The two companies said they will progressively integrate Indian aerospace companies into the C-390 Millennium ecosystem to deliver manufacturing, training and lifecycle support.

Lockheed Martin already has a presence in India — the Indian Air Force currently operates 12 C-130J Super Hercules aircraft. The company says the aircraft it is now offering, the C-130J-30 in its Block 8.1.2 configuration, will be more advanced than the ones currently with the air force.

If it wins, Lockheed has said that 12 aircraft would be built in the U.S. and 48 in India in partnership with Tata Advanced Systems Limited, with which it has a joint venture.

The American company already has a manufacturing base in India. It makes key components, including the aircraft’s empennage or tail assembly, locally with Tata.

Winning the contract would mean establishing a bigger industrial footprint in India, Dan Tenney, Lockheed Martin’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, recently told the Press Trust of India.

“We have a long partnership with Tata that produces components and empennages of the C-130J aircraft. It is a very robust capability that will be expanded in our current bid,” he said.

The company has also proposed upgrading the Indian Air Force’s existing fleet of 12 C-130Js.

India has set a requirement of minimum 40% domestic content for the aircraft. Because the country shares long Himalayan borders with rivals Pakistan and China, the aircraft must also be able to operate in high-altitude locations and from temporary or unpaved strips. Besides ferrying troops, vehicles and ammunition, India also uses military transport aircraft for disaster relief and humanitarian assistance.

The bids are due by early December, after which the proposals will go through technical evaluation.

Amid its two decade-long push for greater local production and technology transfer, the government wants the mega aviation contract to deepen the country’s defense manufacturing footprint.

Turkey’s foreign minister says Ankara weighing Saudi defense support, rules out offensive role

By Reuters

Thursday, Oct 8, 2026

Saudi-backed Yemen government soldiers look on as a pick-up truck drives past near the Jabal Han front, west of the city of Taiz, on Oct. 3, 2026. (Ahmad Al-Basha / AFP via Getty Images)

ANKARA — Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militants under a joint defense pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.

On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defense, electronic warfare and technical support.

“Yemen’s legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them,” Fidan said.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan (R) and Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orban (L) hold joint press conference following their meeting in Ankara, Turkey, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Mustafa Hatipoglu/Anadolu via Getty Images)
“But this is a defensive agreement. When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defense. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory,” he said.

Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia’s operational defense needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make.

On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help its fight with Houthi militants.

Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey’s parliament has not officially ratified the joint defense pact.

Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament’s approval and that they aimed to send it “as soon as possible.”

Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a robust defense industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh’s technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
